Unit 7 of 16 · by Prof. Saurabh

Backpropagation & Automatic Differentiation

Unit 6 ended with a promise: the chain rule becomes matrix multiplication, and that is backpropagation. This unit keeps the promise. You will watch a value flow forward through a graph and its error flow backward; train a single neuron with your own hands and see the loss actually drop; then do a whole layer at once, in matrix form — the exact four formulas inside every deep-learning framework. One backward sweep, and every knob in the network knows which way to turn. And nothing here is taken on faith: every rule the unit leans on is proved on the page, step by step, in plain language.

≈ 80 min read + play 7 interactive widgets · train a neuron live 16 inline checks 🧾 13 proofs, step by step — chain rule, layer formulas, cookbook, checker ✍ 11 solved practice problems
1

The million-knob problem

Imagine this

You are playing darts. Your first throw misses. Your brain notes how far off you were and in which direction — that is the error — and quietly adjusts your stance, grip, and force for the next throw. You learn from the miss. A neural network learns the same way: it makes a prediction (the throw), a loss function measures the miss (the error), and then every parameter gets adjusted to shrink that miss. The question this unit answers: with a million knobs, how does each one find out its own share of the blame — and how can that possibly be cheap?

From Unit 6 you already know what each knob needs: the partial derivative of the loss with respect to that knob. Gradient descent does the rest. So the whole problem is computing a million derivatives, fast.

Try the honest way first, on one small function from the lecture:

f(x)=x2+ex2+cos⁡ ⁣(x2+ex2)f(x)=\sqrt{x^2+e^{x^2}}+\cos\!\big(x^2+e^{x^2}\big)f(x)=x2+ex2​+cos(x2+ex2)

Differentiating by hand, the chain rule sprays copies of 2x+2xex22x+2xe^{x^2}2x+2xex2 everywhere:

dfdx=2x+2xex22x2+ex2−sin⁡ ⁣(x2+ex2)(2x+2xex2)\begin{aligned}\frac{df}{dx}&=\frac{2x+2xe^{x^2}}{2\sqrt{x^2+e^{x^2}}}\\[.3em]&\quad-\sin\!\big(x^2+e^{x^2}\big)\big(2x+2xe^{x^2}\big)\end{aligned}dxdf​​=2x2+ex2​2x+2xex2​−sin(x2+ex2)(2x+2xex2)​

One input, and the expression is already a mouthful — long to write, slow to evaluate, easy to get wrong. Now scale the ambition: a modern network has billions of parameters, and we need the derivative with respect to every one of them, at every training step. Writing formulas by hand is not just impractical — it is impossible.

Backpropagation is the way out, and its two ideas fit in one breath: break the function into baby steps, and send the error backwards through them. Everything else in this unit is those two ideas, carefully.

Pause & predict

A network has a million parameters. Estimating each gradient separately by nudging one parameter and re-running the network would cost about how much?

In one sentence: Training needs the derivative of the loss with respect to every knob, every step — and computing them one at a time would cost a forward pass per knob.
2

Baby steps — the computation graph

Here is the monster function again — but this time we refuse to differentiate it. Instead we just compute it, one baby step at a time, giving each intermediate result a name:

a=x2,b=ea,c=a+b,d=c,e=cos⁡(c),f=d+ea=x^2,\quad b=e^{a},\quad c=a+b,\quad d=\sqrt{c},\quad e=\cos(c),\quad f=d+ea=x2,b=ea,c=a+b,d=c​,e=cos(c),f=d+e

Each step is trivial — a square, an exponential, an addition. Drawn with arrows showing who feeds whom, this is a computation graph, and it is the single most important picture in modern machine learning. Push a number through it, then watch the error walk home:

The graph machineforward: values flow right · backward: blame flows left — press both

Try: press ▶ forward, then use step once to walk the blame back one node at a time — and pause at ccc, where two pieces of blame add.

—

Forward, every node computes one baby step and remembers its value. Backward, every node receives its blame vˉ=∂f/∂v\bar v = \partial f/\partial vvˉ=∂f/∂v — starting from fˉ=1\bar f = 1fˉ​=1 — and passes blame to its parents by multiplying with a local derivative. Watch node ccc: it feeds two children, so its blame arrives in two pieces that add. At the far left, xˉ\bar xxˉ is the answer df/dxdf/dxdf/dx — and the chip checks it against a numerical nudge.

3

The whole algorithm is two rules

In plain words

Rule 1 — along a path, multiply. Each edge of the graph has a local derivative (how much the child moves per unit of parent). Following a path from xxx to fff, the sensitivities multiply — Unit 6's amplifiers in series. Rule 2 — where paths merge, add. If xxx can reach fff by several routes, each route contributes its product, and the contributions add. That is all backpropagation is: multiply along paths, add across paths — organised so no path is ever walked twice.

See both rules in the smallest graph that has two paths — the practice set's own example: f=uvf=uvf=uv with u=x2+yu=x^2+yu=x2+y and v=x−yv=x-yv=x−y. The input xxx reaches fff through uuu and through vvv; click each path and watch its product, then their sum:

Paths multiply, forks addf = uv,  u = x² + y,  v = x − y — two routes from x to f

Try: click route via u, then route via v, then both — and slide xxx to 000 to see one whole route switch off.

Sum: ∂f/∂x=2\partial f/\partial x = 2∂f/∂x=2 — which matches expanding f=x3−x2y+xy−y2f=x^3-x^2y+xy-y^2f=x3−x2y+xy−y2 and differentiating directly. Still at (x,y)=(1,1)(x,y)=(1,1)(x,y)=(1,1): what is ∂f/∂y\partial f/\partial y∂f/∂y? (Routes: y→u→fy\to u\to fy→u→f with ∂u/∂y=1\partial u/\partial y=1∂u/∂y=1, and y→v→fy\to v\to fy→v→f with ∂v/∂y=−1\partial v/\partial y=-1∂v/∂y=−1.)

In one sentence: Backpropagation is exactly two rules — multiply local derivatives along each path, add the paths — applied without ever walking a path twice.
4

Why you can trust the rules — the chain rule, proved

"Multiply along paths, add across paths" has been doing a lot of work, so it had better be true — a theorem, not a slogan. The proof needs exactly one idea, and it is the idea this course keeps returning to: a derivative is a promise about a straight line. Saying "ggg has slope g′(x0)g'(x_0)g′(x0​) at x0x_0x0​" means precisely this:

g(x0+h)=g(x0)+g′(x0) h+r(h),where  r(h)h→0  as h→0.g(x_0+h)=g(x_0)+g'(x_0)\,h+r(h),\qquad\text{where }\ \frac{r(h)}{h}\to 0\ \text{ as }h\to 0.g(x0​+h)=g(x0​)+g′(x0​)h+r(h),where  hr(h)​→0  as h→0.

In words: near x0x_0x0​ the function is a straight line plus a leftover r(h)r(h)r(h) so small that even after dividing by the tiny number hhh, it still shrinks to nothing. That last clause is the entire content of differentiability. Hold on to it — both rules fall out of it in a few lines each.

Pause & predict

The promise demands r(h)/h→0r(h)/h\to0r(h)/h→0, not merely r(h)→0r(h)\to0r(h)→0. What would go wrong if we only asked for r(h)→0r(h)\to0r(h)→0?

Prove it · Rule 1 — along a path, multiply

Claim. If u=g(x)u=g(x)u=g(x) and y=f(u)y=f(u)y=f(u), then at x0x_0x0​ (writing u0=g(x0)u_0=g(x_0)u0​=g(x0​)):  dydx=f′(u0) g′(x0)\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=f'(u_0)\,g'(x_0) dxdy​=f′(u0​)g′(x0​) — the two slopes multiply.

Nothing new — just the definition, applied to ggg.

That is fff's promise, written at u0u_0u0​ with nudge Δu\Delta uΔu: f(u0+Δu)  =  f(u0)+f′(u0) Δu+rf(Δu)f(u_0+\Delta u)\;=\;f(u_0)+f'(u_0)\,\Delta u+r_f(\Delta u)f(u0​+Δu)=f(u0​)+f′(u0​)Δu+rf​(Δu) Same definition, applied to fff. Read off the conclusion. We have shown f(g(x0+h))=f(g(x0))+[f′(u0) g′(x0)] h+R(h),R(h)h→0f\big(g(x_0+h)\big)=f\big(g(x_0)\big)+\big[f'(u_0)\,g'(x_0)\big]\,h+R(h),\qquad \frac{R(h)}{h}\to0f(g(x0​+h))=f(g(x0​))+[f′(u0​)g′(x0​)]h+R(h),hR(h)​→0 — one clean slope, one dying leftover. That is exactly the shape of a derivative's promise, so the number in the bracket is the derivative of the composite. ∎ Two promises composed make a third promise, and slopes multiply while the leftovers stay harmless. "Multiply along a path" is now a theorem.

Now the second rule. Suppose fff reaches the output through several intermediates at once — fff is a function of u1,…,umu_1,\dots,u_mu1​,…,um​, and each uku_kuk​ is a function of xxx. This is precisely the fork situation in the graph: one input, many routes.

Claim.  dfdx=∑k=1m∂f∂uk dukdx\ \dfrac{df}{dx}=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial f}{\partial u_k}\,\frac{du_k}{dx} dxdf​=k=1∑m​∂uk​∂f​dxduk​​ — each route contributes its product, and the contributions add.

Same shape, same conclusion: the composite keeps a promise whose slope is the bracket — the sum over routes of (slope out) × (slope in). ∎ "Add across paths" is not a new fact about graphs. It is what a multi-input derivative means, read one route at a time.
The bridge

The two rules are matrix multiplication in disguise. For vector maps x→Fu→Gy\mathbf x\xrightarrow{F}\mathbf u\xrightarrow{G}\mathbf yxF​uG​y, the chain rule reads JG∘F=JG JFJ_{G\circ F}=J_G\,J_FJG∘F​=JG​JF​ — Jacobians multiply. Now look at one entry of that product, using the row-times-column rule:

(JGJF)ij=∑k(JG)ik(JF)kj\big(J_G J_F\big)_{ij}=\sum_{k}\big(J_G\big)_{ik}\big(J_F\big)_{kj}(JG​JF​)ij​=k∑​(JG​)ik​(JF​)kj​

Each term is one path: input jjj nudges intermediate kkk (that is (JF)kj(J_F)_{kj}(JF​)kj​), which nudges output iii (that is (JG)ik(J_G)_{ik}(JG​)ik​) — multiply along the path. The ∑k\sum_k∑k​ adds one product per intermediate stop — add across paths. The row-times-column rule you have used since Unit 1 is literally the two rules of backpropagation, written at once. Unit 6 promised "the chain rule becomes matrix multiplication"; you have now watched the promise come true, entry by entry.

Pause & predict

In (JGJF)ij=∑k(JG)ik(JF)kj\big(J_G J_F\big)_{ij}=\sum_k (J_G)_{ik}(J_F)_{kj}(JG​JF​)ij​=∑k​(JG​)ik​(JF​)kj​, what is one single term (JG)ik(JF)kj(J_G)_{ik}(J_F)_{kj}(JG​)ik​(JF​)kj​ of the sum, in graph language?

In one sentence: A derivative is a "line plus dying leftover" promise; composing promises multiplies slopes (Rule 1), parallel routes add their products (Rule 2), and matrix multiplication's row-times-column formula is both rules written at once.
5

The recipe, written once and for all

The lecture states the two rules formally, and it is worth reading slowly because this half-line is automatic differentiation. Number every quantity in the graph: x1,…,xdx_1,\dots,x_dx1​,…,xd​ are the inputs, xd+1,…,xD−1x_{d+1},\dots,x_{D-1}xd+1​,…,xD−1​ the intermediate baby steps, xDx_DxD​ the output. Each is computed from its parents by an elementary function:

xi=gi(xPa(xi))x_i = g_i\big(x_{\mathrm{Pa}(x_i)}\big)xi​=gi​(xPa(xi​)​)

Now walk backwards. The output blames itself fully, and every other node collects blame from the nodes it feeds — its children:

∂f∂xD=1,∂f∂xi=∑j: xi∈Pa(xj)∂f∂xj ∂gj∂xi\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_D}=1,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}=\sum_{j:\,x_i\in \mathrm{Pa}(x_j)}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,\frac{\partial g_j}{\partial x_i}∂xD​∂f​=1,∂xi​∂f​=j:xi​∈Pa(xj​)∑​∂xj​∂f​∂xi​∂gj​​

Read it like a postal system: node jjj already knows its own blame ∂f/∂xj\partial f/\partial x_j∂f/∂xj​. It mails each parent iii a copy, scaled by the local derivative ∂gj/∂xi\partial g_j/\partial x_i∂gj​/∂xi​ of its own baby step. A parent with several children just adds up its mail. One sweep from right to left and every node in the graph — every input, every weight — holds its derivative.

Two things make this cheap. Each blame ∂f/∂xj\partial f/\partial x_j∂f/∂xj​ is computed once and reused by all of jjj's parents. And each local derivative ∂gj/∂xi\partial g_j/\partial x_i∂gj​/∂xi​ is trivial, because each baby step is trivial — the derivative of eae^aea or c\sqrt cc​ or a+ba+ba+b, never of the whole monster. This is why the lecture can conclude: computing all the derivatives costs about the same as computing the function itself.

Prove it · the recipe is correct

Claim. Process the nodes from right to left; then the recipe's xˉi\bar x_ixˉi​ equals the true ∂f/∂xi\partial f/\partial x_i∂f/∂xi​ for every node in the graph.

1
Base case. The rightmost node: xˉD=1=∂f/∂f\bar x_D=1=\partial f/\partial fxˉD​=1=∂f/∂f — the output's sensitivity to itself. Nudge fff by hhh and fff changes by hhh. Slope 1, no leftover at all.
2
The order does the bookkeeping. Working right to left means: by the time we reach node xix_ixi​, every child xjx_jxj​ (every node that uses xix_ixi​) has already been processed and — by induction — already holds its correct blame xˉj=∂f/∂xj\bar x_j=\partial f/\partial x_jxˉj​=∂f/∂xj​. Children sit to the right of their parents in the graph, so a right-to-left sweep always finds the mail ready before it must be sent.
3
Apply Rule 2 at node xix_ixi​, with its children as the intermediates. Any nudge of xix_ixi​ can reach fff only through the children, so §4's theorem says ∂f∂xi=∑j: xi∈Pa(xj)∂f∂xj ∂gj∂xi\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}=\sum_{j:\,x_i\in\mathrm{Pa}(x_j)}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,\frac{\partial g_j}{\partial x_i}∂xi​∂f​=j:xi​∈Pa(xj​)∑​∂xj​∂f​∂xi​∂gj​​ — and every factor on the right is one the recipe possesses: the child's (already correct) blame, times the local slope of the child's baby step. So the value the recipe writes into xˉi\bar x_ixˉi​ is the true derivative. Right-to-left induction covers the whole graph. ∎ The recipe is not a new algorithm to take on trust — it is Rule 2, applied once per node, in an order that guarantees the mail is always ready.
Pause & predict

In the recipe, the sum for ∂f/∂xi\partial f/\partial x_i∂f/∂xi​ runs over the children of xix_ixi​ — the nodes that use it. Why children, not parents?

In one sentence: Set fˉ=1\bar f=1fˉ​=1, then let every node mail each parent its own blame times a local derivative — one right-to-left sweep prices every knob.
6

One neuron, trained by your own hands

Time to point this machinery at something that learns. The smallest possible network: one neuron with one weight www and one bias bbb, one input xxx, one target yyy:

z=wx+b,a=tanh⁡(z),L=12 (a−y)2z=wx+b,\qquad a=\tanh(z),\qquad L=\tfrac12\,(a-y)^2z=wx+b,a=tanh(z),L=21​(a−y)2

Forward: three baby steps to the loss. Backward: the blame walks home through the same three steps. The key arrival is δ=∂L/∂z\delta=\partial L/\partial zδ=∂L/∂z — the blame reaching the pre-activation — because every parameter feeding zzz then reads its gradient straight off δ\deltaδ: ∂L/∂w=δ x\partial L/\partial w=\delta\,x∂L/∂w=δx, ∂L/∂b=δ\partial L/\partial b=\delta∂L/∂b=δ, ∂L/∂x=δ w\partial L/\partial x=\delta\,w∂L/∂x=δw. Compute δ\deltaδ once, hand out copies. Then take an actual gradient step and watch the loss fall:

The learning neuronforward → backward → step, repeat — this is training, complete

Try: predict the sign of δ\deltaδ before each step; then set the target to y=−1y=-1y=−1 and watch the same machinery push www the other way.

A whole layer at once — backprop in matrix form

A real layer is the same neuron, vectorised: mmm neurons share the input vector x∈Rn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^nx∈Rn,

Z=Ax+b,a=σ(Z)Z=A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b},\qquad \mathbf{a}=\sigma(Z)Z=Ax+b,a=σ(Z)

with A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n the weights, b∈Rm\mathbf b\in\mathbb{R}^mb∈Rm the biases, and the sigmoid σ(z)=11+e−z\sigma(z)=\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}σ(z)=1+e−z1​ applied entry by entry. The blame arriving from above is δ(a)=∂Loss/∂a\boldsymbol\delta^{(a)}=\partial\mathrm{Loss}/\partial \mathbf aδ(a)=∂Loss/∂a, one entry per neuron.

Read the answer as people first, then as symbols. Passing blame back through the layer gives four lines. Through the sigmoid: each neuron's blame is scaled by its own slope — no mixing between neurons. A weight: gets the blame of its neuron times the activity of its input — big only when both are big. A bias: gets its neuron's blame straight. The input: gets blame collected back through the weights, and that becomes the mail for the layer below.

Now the symbols. Step one, through the sigmoid: ai=σ(Zi)a_i=\sigma(Z_i)ai​=σ(Zi​) touches only its own ZiZ_iZi​, so the Jacobian ∂a/∂Z\partial\mathbf a/\partial Z∂a/∂Z is diagonal — diag⁡ ⁣(a⊙(1−a))\operatorname{diag}\!\big(\mathbf a\odot(1-\mathbf a)\big)diag(a⊙(1−a)), using σ′=σ(1−σ)\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)σ′=σ(1−σ) — and the blame is scaled entrywise (⊙\odot⊙ is the Hadamard, entrywise, product):

δ(Z)=δ(a)⊙a⊙(1−a)\boldsymbol\delta^{(Z)}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(a)}\odot \mathbf a\odot(1-\mathbf a)δ(Z)=δ(a)⊙a⊙(1−a)

Step two, through Z=Ax+bZ=A\mathbf x+\mathbf bZ=Ax+b. Since Zi=∑jAijxj+biZ_i=\sum_j A_{ij}x_j+b_iZi​=∑j​Aij​xj​+bi​, each weight sees ∂Zi/∂Aij=xj\partial Z_i/\partial A_{ij}=x_j∂Zi​/∂Aij​=xj​, and the chain rule assembles into three matrix formulas:

∂Loss∂A=δ(Z)x⊤,∂Loss∂b=δ(Z),∂Loss∂x=A⊤δ(Z)\begin{gathered}\frac{\partial\mathrm{Loss}}{\partial A}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(Z)}\mathbf{x}^{\top},\qquad \frac{\partial\mathrm{Loss}}{\partial \mathbf b}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(Z)},\\[.4em] \frac{\partial\mathrm{Loss}}{\partial \mathbf x}=A^{\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(Z)}\end{gathered}∂A∂Loss​=δ(Z)x⊤,∂b∂Loss​=δ(Z),∂x∂Loss​=A⊤δ(Z)​

The weights: δ(Z)x⊤\boldsymbol\delta^{(Z)}\mathbf x^\topδ(Z)x⊤ is an outer product — blame of my row, times activity of my column. The biases: the blame itself. The input: A⊤δ(Z)A^\top\boldsymbol\delta^{(Z)}A⊤δ(Z) re-mixes the blame back through the transposed weights — and this vector is precisely the δ(a)\boldsymbol\delta^{(a)}δ(a) the previous layer receives as its mail. Layer after layer, the same four lines: that is deep learning's inner loop.

Claim. σ(z)=11+e−z\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}σ(z)=1+e−z1​ satisfies σ′=σ(1−σ)\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)σ′=σ(1−σ) — so the backward pass needs no new function evaluations.

1
Differentiate with Rule 1: σ=(1+e−z)−1\sigma=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}σ=(1+e−z)−1, outer slope −(1+e−z)−2-(1+e^{-z})^{-2}−(1+e−z)−2, inner slope −e−z ⁣:-e^{-z}\!:−e−z: σ′=−(1+e−z)−2⋅(−e−z)=e−z(1+e−z)2\sigma'=-(1+e^{-z})^{-2}\cdot(-e^{-z})=\frac{e^{-z}}{(1+e^{-z})^{2}}σ′=−(1+e−z)−2⋅(−e−z)=(1+e−z)2e−z​ The two minus signs cancel — sigmoid always rises.
2
Split the fraction into two factors you can recognise: e−z(1+e−z)2=11+e−z⏟= σ⋅e−z1+e−z⏟= 1−σsince1−σ=(1+e−z)−11+e−z=e−z1+e−z\frac{e^{-z}}{(1+e^{-z})^{2}}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}}_{=\ \sigma}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}}_{=\ 1-\sigma} \qquad\text{since}\quad 1-\sigma=\frac{(1+e^{-z})-1}{1+e^{-z}}=\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}(1+e−z)2e−z​== σ1+e−z1​​​⋅= 1−σ1+e−ze−z​​​since1−σ=1+e−z(1+e−z)−1​=1+e−ze−z​ So σ′=σ(1−σ)\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)σ′=σ(1−σ). ∎ Output in, derivative out: a⊙(1−a)\mathbf a\odot(1-\mathbf a)a⊙(1−a) uses only the a\mathbf aa the forward pass cached. Who depends on whom. ai=σ(Zi)a_i=\sigma(Z_i)ai​=σ(Zi​) reads exactly one input, ZiZ_iZi​. The diagonal. The gradient cookbook — five identities you'll use forever

Backprop needs local derivatives, and in matrix land a handful of them cover almost everything. The lecture lists five; learn them as sentences, not just symbols. (Gradients here are rows, Unit 6's convention.)

IdentitySay it in words
∂ x⊤a∂x=a⊤\dfrac{\partial\, \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{a}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{a}^{\top}∂x∂x⊤a​=a⊤a dot product's sensitivity to x\mathbf xx is just the other vector
∂ a⊤x∂x=a⊤\dfrac{\partial\, \mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{x}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{a}^{\top}∂x∂a⊤x​=a⊤same thing — a dot product doesn't care about the order
∂ a⊤Xb∂X=ab⊤\dfrac{\partial\, \mathbf{a}^{\top}X\mathbf{b}}{\partial X}=\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}^{\top}∂X∂a⊤Xb​=ab⊤each entry XijX_{ij}Xij​ is multiplied by aibja_i b_jai​bj​ — so the gradient is that outer product
∂ x⊤Bx∂x=x⊤ ⁣(B+B⊤)\dfrac{\partial\, \mathbf{x}^{\top}B\mathbf{x}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\!\big(B+B^{\top}\big)∂x∂x⊤Bx​=x⊤(B+B⊤)x\mathbf xx appears twice, so you get two copies — BBB once from each side
∂∂s(x−As)⊤W(x−As)=−2(x−As)⊤WA\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{s}}(\mathbf x-A\mathbf s)^{\top}W(\mathbf x-A\mathbf s)=-2(\mathbf x-A\mathbf s)^{\top}WA∂s∂​(x−As)⊤W(x−As)=−2(x−As)⊤WAfor symmetric WWW: least-squares' own gradient — chain rule through the residual

Notice the family resemblance to Section 7: the third identity is why ∂Loss/∂A\partial\mathrm{Loss}/\partial A∂Loss/∂A came out as an outer product, and the last one is the loss ∥y−As∥2\|\mathbf y-A\mathbf s\|^2∥y−As∥2 that trains linear models — you will meet it again the moment optimisation starts in Unit 9. Below, every identity is derived in full — the whole cookbook takes four short arguments. The arena's Problem 7 re-checks two of them with concrete numbers, and Problem 10 puts the cookbook to work on a real model.

Prove it · the whole cookbook, four short derivations

Claim. Every identity in the table is entry-wise differentiation, organised. The method is always the same: find every appearance of the variable, add one term per appearance.

1
Dot product. x⊤a=∑ixiai\mathbf x^{\top}\mathbf a=\sum_i x_i a_ix⊤a=∑i​xi​ai​. Differentiate with respect to one coordinate xk ⁣:x_k\!:xk​: every term is constant except xkakx_k a_kxk​ak​, whose slope is aka_kak​. Collect the coordinates into a row: ∂(x⊤a)∂x=a⊤\frac{\partial(\mathbf x^{\top}\mathbf a)}{\partial\mathbf x}=\mathbf a^{\top}∂x∂(x⊤a)​=a⊤ And a⊤x\mathbf a^{\top}\mathbf xa⊤x is the same scalar, so the table's second line comes free.
2
The sandwich. a⊤Xb=∑i,jaiXijbj\mathbf a^{\top}X\mathbf b=\sum_{i,j}a_i X_{ij}b_ja⊤Xb=∑i,j​ai​Xij​bj​. The entry XijX_{ij}Xij​ appears once, with coefficient aibj ⁣:a_ib_j\!:ai​bj​: ∂(a⊤Xb)∂Xij=aibj⇒∂(a⊤Xb)∂X=ab⊤\frac{\partial(\mathbf a^{\top}X\mathbf b)}{\partial X_{ij}}=a_ib_j\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\partial(\mathbf a^{\top}X\mathbf b)}{\partial X}=\mathbf a\mathbf b^{\top}∂Xij​∂(a⊤Xb)​=ai​bj​⇒∂X∂(a⊤Xb)​=ab⊤ The same one-appearance argument that made ∂L/∂A\partial L/\partial A∂L/∂A an outer product in the layer proof — it is literally the same fact.
3
The quadratic — where B+B⊤B+B^{\top}B+B⊤ is born. x⊤Bx=∑i,jBij xi xj\mathbf x^{\top}B\mathbf x=\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}\,x_i\,x_jx⊤Bx=∑i,j​Bij​xi​xj​, and x\mathbf xx appears twice in each term. Product rule on xixjx_ix_jxi​xj​, with respect to xkx_kxk​: the left copy fires when i=ki=ki=k, contributing ∑jBkjxj=(Bx)k\sum_j B_{kj}x_j=(B\mathbf x)_k∑j​Bkj​xj​=(Bx)k​; the right copy fires when j=kj=kj=k, contributing ∑iBikxi=(B⊤x)k\sum_i B_{ik}x_i=(B^{\top}\mathbf x)_k∑i​Bik​xi​=(B⊤x)k​. Add the two: ∂(x⊤Bx)∂xk=(Bx)k+(B⊤x)k⇒∂(x⊤Bx)∂x=x⊤(B+B⊤)\frac{\partial(\mathbf x^{\top}B\mathbf x)}{\partial x_k}=(B\mathbf x)_k+(B^{\top}\mathbf x)_k\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\partial(\mathbf x^{\top}B\mathbf x)}{\partial\mathbf x}=\mathbf x^{\top}\big(B+B^{\top}\big)∂xk​∂(x⊤Bx)​=(Bx)k​+(B⊤x)k​⇒∂x∂(x⊤Bx)​=x⊤(B+B⊤) Two appearances of x\mathbf xx, two donated terms — the "mysterious" +B⊤+B^{\top}+B⊤ is Rule 2's fork, hiding in plain algebra. For symmetric BBB it collapses to 2x⊤B2\mathbf x^{\top}B2x⊤B.

Look at the shape of those formulas: each one is the previous one's product, extended by one factor. Computed naively, left to right every time, you would rebuild the same long prefix over and over. Computed once from the loss end — keeping the running product as the δ\boldsymbol\deltaδ that Section 7 handed backwards — every factor in the whole triangle is touched exactly once:

Claim. The chain ∂L∂f1=∂L∂fK ∂fK∂fK−1⋯∂f2∂f1\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial f_1}=\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial f_K}\,\dfrac{\partial f_K}{\partial f_{K-1}}\cdots\dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial f_1}∂f1​∂L​=∂fK​∂L​∂fK−1​∂fK​​⋯∂f1​∂f2​​ can be multiplied in either order. 4
Same factors, same answer, wildly different bill. Keeping the scalar-loss end first means every step is a cheap row-times-matrix product. That choice of order is reverse-mode automatic differentiation. ∎ And it explains the fine print to come: reverse mode wins because training has ONE output (the loss) and millions of inputs. Flip that ratio and the other order — forward mode — wins instead.

Fine print worth knowing

Three ways to differentiate, only one scales. Symbolic differentiation (what you do on paper, what algebra systems do) produces exact formulas — which explode in size for deep compositions. Numerical differentiation nudges the input and divides — one pass per parameter, plus a precision trap you can see below. Automatic differentiation — this unit — is a third thing: exact like symbolic, cheap like a function call, because it differentiates the program, step by step, instead of the formula.

The precision trap. A finite difference f(x+h)−f(x−h)2h\tfrac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}2hf(x+h)−f(x−h)​ has two enemies. Big hhh: the secant misses the tangent (Unit 6's curvature gap). Tiny hhh: the computer subtracts two nearly equal numbers and the difference drowns in rounding error. Squeeze hhh yourself:

The gradient checkerfinite differences vs. the exact answer — there is a best h, and it is not 0

Try: slide hhh down one decade at a time and watch the error fall 100× per decade — until, near 10−610^{-6}10−6, it stops and turns.

Frameworks still use this as a gradient checker — a sanity test for hand-written backward passes — but never for training.

That is the entire case for automatic differentiation, compressed into one minimisation.

σ′\sigma' σ′ is free. The identity σ′=σ(1−σ)\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)σ′=σ(1−σ) means the backward pass needs no new function calls — the forward pass already computed a\mathbf aa, and a⊙(1−a)\mathbf a\odot(1-\mathbf a)a⊙(1−a) is two cheap operations. The same trick works for tanh⁡\tanhtanh (1−a21-a^21−a2). Frameworks cache activations on the way forward precisely so the way back is arithmetic only — that cache is the "memory cost of training".

Vanishing gradients, revisited. Each sigmoid layer multiplies the blame by a⊙(1−a)≤14\mathbf a\odot(1-\mathbf a)\le\tfrac14a⊙(1−a)≤41​. Fifty layers deep, the blame arriving at layer one has passed fifty such factors — Unit 6's gears compounding — which is why early deep networks would not train, and why ReLU (slope 1 where active) took over.

Reverse is for losses; forward exists too. Everything here swept blame backwards, which prices all inputs of one output — perfect for a scalar loss. There is a mirror-image forward mode that prices all outputs of one input; it wins only when outputs vastly outnumber inputs, which training never is. That is why every deep-learning framework is a reverse-mode machine.

Pause & predict

In the gradient checker, why does making hhh ever smaller eventually make the estimate worse?

Forward mode you can hold in your hand — dual numbers. Reverse mode swept blame backwards. Forward mode has an algebraic form so tidy you can run it with pencil and paper: carry every quantity as a pair — its value and its derivative — and teach ordinary arithmetic to update both at once.

Run the program on pairs, seeding the input as x=x0+1⋅εx=x_0+1\cdot\varepsilonx=x0​+1⋅ε (its derivative with respect to itself is 1). Example — f(x)=x exf(x)=x\,e^{x}f(x)=xex at x0=1x_0=1x0​=1: x=(1, 1) → ex  (e, e) → × x  (1⋅e,  1⋅e+1⋅e)=(e, 2e)x=(1,\,1)\ \xrightarrow{\ e^{x}\ }\ (e,\,e)\ \xrightarrow{\ \times\, x\ }\ \big(1\cdot e,\ \ 1\cdot e+1\cdot e\big)=(e,\,2e)x=(1,1)  ex ​ (e,e)  ×x ​ (1⋅e,  1⋅e+1⋅e)=(e,2e) So f(1)=ef(1)=ef(1)=e and f′(1)=2e≈5.4366f'(1)=2e\approx5.4366f′(1)=2e≈5.4366 — exact, and no derivative formula was ever written down. ∎ Check: f′=ex(1+x)f'=e^{x}(1+x)f′=ex(1+x) gives 2e2e2e. ✓ This is forward-mode autodiff: one sweep prices all outputs of one input — the mirror image of backprop, and the winner when inputs are few and outputs many.
Pause & predict

The single rule ε2=0\varepsilon^{2}=0ε2=0 makes the product rule appear on its own. What is ε2=0\varepsilon^{2}=0ε2=0 really encoding?

In one sentence: Autodiff is exact like symbolic and cheap like numerical with neither one's flaw — and the finite-difference valley is why "just use tiny h" was never an option.
12

What to carry forward

One picture generated this entire unit: a function drawn as a graph of baby steps, with values flowing right and blame flowing left. Everything else was careful bookkeeping on that picture.

The one thing to remember

Blame flows backwards through the same graph that computed the value. Multiply along paths, add at forks, reuse every partial product — and a million derivatives cost one sweep. When a framework call like loss.backward() feels like magic, it is exactly this unit, executed by a for-loop.

13

Practice arena — the unit's problem set, solved in full

Eleven problems: three from Part C of Prof. Saurabh's practice set (Parts A and B — Taylor series and the Hessian — belong to Unit 8's territory and wait there), three from his companion guide, and five written for this arena — the identity drill (Problem 7), the complete numeric backward pass (Problem 8), and three proof workouts (Problems 9–11) that derive from scratch the rules this unit leaned on. Every solution below is machine-verified.

One habit does most of the work: draw the graph first, then walk it backwards — multiply along paths, add at forks, and check every shape before trusting any algebra.

Problem 1medium

A one-layer network computes z=Wx\mathbf z=W\mathbf xz=Wx and the loss g(z)=12∥z−t∥2g(\mathbf z)=\tfrac12\|\mathbf z-\mathbf t\|^2g(z)=21​∥z−t∥2 against a target t\mathbf tt, with W=[1201−11],x=[11],t=[102].W=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf t=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}.W=​10−1​211​​,x=[11​],t=​102​​. (a) Compute ∇z g\nabla_{\mathbf z}\,g∇z​g (with its dimension) and J=∂z/∂xJ=\partial\mathbf z/\partial\mathbf xJ=∂z/∂x (with its dimension). (b) Combine them to get ∇x g\nabla_{\mathbf x}\,g∇x​g, and give the loss value.

What this tests. One honest backward step through a linear layer: the upstream gradient is the residual, and it returns to the input through W⊤W^{\top}W⊤.

Step 1 — forward pass. z=Wx=(1+2, 0+1, −1+1)⊤=(3,1,0)⊤\mathbf z=W\mathbf x=(1{+}2,\ 0{+}1,\ -1{+}1)^{\top}=(3,1,0)^{\top}z=Wx=(1+2, 0+1, −1+1)⊤=(3,1,0)⊤. Residual r=z−t=(2,1,−2)⊤\mathbf r=\mathbf z-\mathbf t=(2,1,-2)^{\top}r=z−t=(2,1,−2)⊤, and the loss is g=12(22+12+(−2)2)=92=4.5g=\tfrac12(2^2+1^2+(-2)^2)=\tfrac92=4.5g=21​(22+12+(−2)2)=29​=4.5.
(a) Step 2 — gradient at the output. For g=12∥z−t∥2g=\tfrac12\|\mathbf z-\mathbf t\|^2g=21​∥z−t∥2,  ∇z g=z−t=r=(2,1,−2)⊤\ \nabla_{\mathbf z}\,g=\mathbf z-\mathbf t=\mathbf r=(2,1,-2)^{\top} ∇z​g=z−t=r=(2,1,−2)⊤ — dimension 3×13\times13×1, one entry per output. The Jacobian of a linear map is the matrix itself: J=∂(Wx)/∂x=WJ=\partial(W\mathbf x)/\partial\mathbf x=WJ=∂(Wx)/∂x=W, dimension 3×23\times23×2 (outputs × inputs).
(b) Step 3 — chain them. ∇x g=J⊤∇z g=W⊤r=[10−1211][21−2]=[1⋅2+0⋅1+(−1)(−2)2⋅2+1⋅1+1⋅(−2)]=[43]\nabla_{\mathbf x}\,g=J^{\top}\nabla_{\mathbf z}\,g=W^{\top}\mathbf r=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\2&1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot2+0\cdot1+(-1)(-2)\\2\cdot2+1\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix}∇x​g=J⊤∇z​g=W⊤r=[12​01​−11​]​21−2​​=[1⋅2+0⋅1+(−1)(−2)2⋅2+1⋅1+1⋅(−2)​]=[43​] Dimension check: ∇zg\nabla_{\mathbf z}g∇z​g is 3×13\times13×1, W⊤W^{\top}W⊤ is 2×32\times32×3, product 2×12\times12×1 — the shape of x\mathbf xx, as a gradient must be. ✓

∇zg=(2,1,−2)⊤\nabla_{\mathbf z}g=(2,1,-2)^{\top}∇z​g=(2,1,−2)⊤ (3×1), J=WJ=WJ=W (3×2), ∇xg=(4,3)⊤\nabla_{\mathbf x}g=(4,3)^{\top}∇x​g=(4,3)⊤ (2×1), loss =4.5=4.5=4.5.

Remember

"Backprop through a linear layer" = "multiply the incoming gradient by W⊤W^{\top}W⊤". You can also check by substituting first: g(x)=12∥Wx−t∥2g(\mathbf x)=\tfrac12\|W\mathbf x-\mathbf t\|^2g(x)=21​∥Wx−t∥2 has gradient W⊤(Wx−t)=W⊤rW^{\top}(W\mathbf x-\mathbf t)=W^{\top}\mathbf rW⊤(Wx−t)=W⊤r — same answer, one line.

Problem 4hard

Define g(z,ν):=log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡q(z,ν)g(\mathbf z,\boldsymbol\nu):=\log p(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)-\log q(\mathbf z,\boldsymbol\nu)g(z,ν):=logp(x,z)−logq(z,ν) with z:=t(ϵ,ν)\mathbf z:=t(\boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\nu)z:=t(ϵ,ν), for differentiable functions p,q,tp,q,tp,q,t and x∈RD, z∈RE, ν∈RF, ϵ∈RG\mathbf x\in\mathbb{R}^D,\ \mathbf z\in\mathbb{R}^E,\ \boldsymbol\nu\in\mathbb{R}^F,\ \boldsymbol\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}^Gx∈RD, z∈RE, ν∈RF, ϵ∈RG. What this tests. Direct and indirect paths of influence — the multivariate chain rule when a variable appears both explicitly and through an intermediate. (This is the gradient inside variational autoencoders.)

Show the full solution
Step 1 — draw the graph. ν\boldsymbol\nuν reaches ggg two ways: directly (it sits inside log⁡q(z,ν)\log q(\mathbf z,\boldsymbol\nu)logq(z,ν)) and indirectly (it builds z=t(ϵ,ν)\mathbf z=t(\boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\nu)z=t(ϵ,ν), and z\mathbf zz feeds both log⁡p\log plogp and log⁡q\log qlogq). Total derivative = sum over both routes.
Step 2 — the direct route. Hold z\mathbf zz fixed and differentiate ggg in the ν\boldsymbol\nuν-slot only. The log⁡p\log plogp term has no direct ν\boldsymbol\nuν: ∂g∂ν=−∂log⁡q(z,ν)∂ν(1×F)\frac{\partial g}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}=-\frac{\partial \log q(\mathbf z,\boldsymbol\nu)}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}\qquad(1\times F)∂ν∂g​=−∂ν∂logq(z,ν)​(1×F)
Step 3 — the indirect route, two links. First how ggg feels z\mathbf zz, then how z\mathbf zz feels ν\boldsymbol\nuν: ∂g∂z=∂log⁡p(x,z)∂z−∂log⁡q(z,ν)∂z(1×E),∂z∂ν=∂t(ϵ,ν)∂ν(E×F)\frac{\partial g}{\partial\mathbf z}=\frac{\partial \log p(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)}{\partial\mathbf z}-\frac{\partial \log q(\mathbf z,\boldsymbol\nu)}{\partial\mathbf z}\quad(1\times E),\qquad \frac{\partial\mathbf z}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}=\frac{\partial t(\boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\nu)}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}\quad(E\times F)∂z∂g​=∂z∂logp(x,z)​−∂z∂logq(z,ν)​(1×E),∂ν∂z​=∂ν∂t(ϵ,ν)​(E×F)
Step 4 — add the routes. dgdν=−∂log⁡q∂ν  +  (∂log⁡p∂z−∂log⁡q∂z)∂t∂ν\frac{d g}{d\boldsymbol\nu}=-\frac{\partial \log q}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}\;+\;\left(\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial\mathbf z}-\frac{\partial \log q}{\partial\mathbf z}\right)\frac{\partial t}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}dνdg​=−∂ν∂logq​+(∂z∂logp​−∂z∂logq​)∂ν∂t​ Dimension check: (1×F)+(1×E)(E×F)=(1×F)(1\times F)+(1\times E)(E\times F)=(1\times F)(1×F)+(1×E)(E×F)=(1×F) ✓.

Problem 6medium

Compute dfdx\dfrac{d\mathbf f}{d\mathbf x}dxdf​ for f(z)=sin⁡(z)\mathbf f(\mathbf z)=\sin(\mathbf z)f(z)=sin(z) applied entrywise,  z=Ax+b\ \mathbf z=A\mathbf x+\mathbf b z=Ax+b, with A∈RE×D, x∈RD, b∈REA\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times D},\ \mathbf x\in\mathbb{R}^{D},\ \mathbf b\in\mathbb{R}^{E}A∈RE×D, x∈RD, b∈RE. State every dimension.

What this tests. The Jacobian chain rule with an entrywise nonlinearity — the exact structure of Section 7's layer, with sin⁡\sinsin in place of σ\sigmaσ.

Show the full solution

The activation family, from first principles. (a) Show that the softplus s(z)=ln⁡(1+ez)s(z)=\ln(1+e^{z})s(z)=ln(1+ez) has derivative s′(z)=σ(z)s'(z)=\sigma(z)s′(z)=σ(z) — the sigmoid is softplus's slope. (b) Prove the bridge tanh⁡(z)=2 σ(2z)−1\tanh(z)=2\,\sigma(2z)-1tanh(z)=2σ(2z)−1. (c) Using (b) and σ′=σ(1−σ)\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)σ′=σ(1−σ), derive tanh⁡′=1−tanh⁡2\tanh'=1-\tanh^{2}tanh′=1−tanh2 without a quotient rule.

What this tests. That the activation identities frameworks hard-code are a small connected family — one proof engine (find the appearances, chain the slopes) generates them all.

Show the full solution
(a) Chain rule through the logarithm. Outer slope 1/(1+ez)1/(1+e^{z})1/(1+ez), inner slope eze^{z}ez: s′(z)=ez1+ez=1e−z+1=σ(z) ✓s'(z)=\frac{e^{z}}{1+e^{z}}=\frac{1}{e^{-z}+1}=\sigma(z)\ \checkmarks′(z)=1+ezez​=e−z+11​=σ(z) ✓ (dividing top and bottom by eze^{z}ez in the middle step). So the smooth ramp softplus steepens exactly at the sigmoid's rate — which is why σ\sigmaσ is also called the logistic function.
(b) Build 2σ(2z)−12\sigma(2z)-12σ(2z)−1 and simplify. 2 σ(2z)−1=21+e−2z−1=2−(1+e−2z)1+e−2z=1−e−2z1+e−2z2\,\sigma(2z)-1=\frac{2}{1+e^{-2z}}-1=\frac{2-(1+e^{-2z})}{1+e^{-2z}}=\frac{1-e^{-2z}}{1+e^{-2z}}2σ(2z)−1=1+e−2z2​−1=1+e−2z2−(1+e−2z)​=1+e−2z1−e−2z​ Multiply top and bottom by eze^{z}ez: ez−e−zez+e−z=tanh⁡(z) ✓\frac{e^{z}-e^{-z}}{e^{z}+e^{-z}}=\tanh(z)\ \checkmarkez+e−zez−e−z​=tanh(z) ✓ In words: tanh is a sigmoid, stretched to run twice as fast and re-centred to fill (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1).
(c) Differentiate the bridge with Rule 1. Write t=tanh⁡zt=\tanh zt=tanhz and note from (b) that σ(2z)=1+t2\sigma(2z)=\tfrac{1+t}{2}σ(2z)=21+t​, hence 1−σ(2z)=1−t21-\sigma(2z)=\tfrac{1-t}{2}1−σ(2z)=21−t​. Then tanh⁡′(z)=2⋅σ′(2z)⋅2=4 σ(2z)(1−σ(2z))=4⋅1+t2⋅1−t2=(1+t)(1−t)=1−t2 ✓\tanh'(z)=2\cdot\sigma'(2z)\cdot 2=4\,\sigma(2z)\big(1-\sigma(2z)\big)=4\cdot\frac{1+t}{2}\cdot\frac{1-t}{2}=(1+t)(1-t)=1-t^{2}\ \checkmarktanh′(z)=2⋅σ′(2z)⋅2=4σ(2z)(1−σ(2z))=4⋅21+t​⋅21−t​=(1+t)(1−t)=1−t2 ✓ — the factor 222 outside is the bridge's scaling, the factor 222 inside is the chain rule through 2z2z2z.

s′=σs'=\sigmas′=σ;  tanh⁡z=2σ(2z)−1\ \tanh z=2\sigma(2z)-1 tanhz=2σ(2z)−1;  tanh⁡′=1−tanh⁡2\ \tanh'=1-\tanh^{2} tanh′=1−tanh2, derived purely from σ′=σ(1−σ)\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)σ′=σ(1−σ).

Remember

All three facts are one family portrait: softplus's slope is σ\sigmaσ, tanh⁡\tanhtanh is a rescaled σ\sigmaσ, and both backward-pass identities (σ(1−σ)\sigma(1-\sigma)σ(1−σ) and 1−a21-a^21−a2) are the same identity seen through the bridge. Knowing one buys you the others.

The widget's tangent line and this pencil-and-paper pair computation are the same mathematics arriving by two roads.
(c) Why exact. No step ever subtracts two nearly equal numbers or divides by a small hhh — each rule (sum, product, g′(a)a˙g'(a)\dot ag′(a)a˙) is the corresponding calculus rule, applied with ordinary arithmetic — so the only error anywhere is standard floating-point rounding of the values themselves.

(a) (e, 3e)(e,\,3e)(e,3e): f′(1)=3e≈8.1548f'(1)=3e\approx8.1548f′(1)=3e≈8.1548. (b) (5, −0.8)(5,\,-0.8)(5,−0.8): f′(−4)=−45f'(-4)=-\tfrac45f′(−4)=−54​. (c) The algebra rules are the calculus rules — nothing is approximated, so nothing needs a step size.

Remember

Reverse mode (this unit's hero) and dual numbers (its mirror) bracket the field: backward for one output and many inputs, forward for one input and many outputs. Both differentiate the program, both are exact — and neither ever writes a derivative formula.
